lead: Microwave energy has to be split, coupled, controlled, generated and measured. These chapters show how, so that you can read S-parameters, analyse tees, couplers and dividers, choose ferrite devices and microwave sources, and interpret VSWR, power and network-analyser measurements.
about: The unit starts with S-parameters (4.1), the wave language used for every microwave component. Waveguide tees (4.2) apply that language to three- and four-port junctions, and directional couplers and hybrid rings (4.3) extend it to power sampling and phase splitting. Power dividers and attenuators (4.4) give controlled splitting and level control. Ferrite devices (4.5) add nonreciprocal isolation, circulation and phase shift. Microwave tubes (4.6) and solid-state sources (4.7) cover generation and amplification from high-power beams to low-voltage diodes. Microwave measurements (4.8) show how VSWR, power, frequency and S-parameters are measured. Microwave integrated circuits and MMIC (4.9) put the components on a substrate as a compact circuit.

chapters.idea: At microwave frequencies, components are described by waves travelling in and out of ports, collected in the scattering matrix.
chapters.depth: Define incident wave aᵢ and reflected wave bᵢ at port i, with Sᵢⱼ = bᵢ/aⱼ when all ports except j are matched to Z₀. Cover 2-port meanings of S₁₁, S₂₁, S₁₂, S₂₂; return loss, insertion loss, VSWR; reciprocity S = Sᵀ; losslessness S†S = I; matched condition; reference plane and frequency dependence. Some syllabi call this the scattering matrix. Show the signal-flow graph; do not derive full N-port algebra.

figure.aria: Signal-flow graph of a two-port: incident waves a₁ and a₂ produce reflected waves b₁ and b₂ through the four S-parameters.

chapters.example: A 50 Ω two-port at 10 GHz has S₁₁ = 0.2∠0°, S₂₁ = 0.9∠−30°, S₁₂ = 0, S₂₂ = 0.1∠0°. Find the return loss at port 1, the insertion loss, the input VSWR when port 2 is matched, and the reverse isolation. Answer: RL = −20 log₁₀(0.2) = 13.98 dB; insertion loss = −20 log₁₀(0.9) = 0.92 dB; VSWR = (1+0.2)/(1−0.2) = 1.5; S₁₂ = 0 gives infinite isolation.
chapters.trap: Using |S₂₁| directly as dB gain; forgetting all other ports must be matched; ignoring reference impedance and reference plane.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1: transmission lines, reflection coefficient, VSWR.
chapters.leave: Leave component S-matrices to 4.2–4.5 and VNA calibration to 4.8.

chapters.idea: A waveguide tee splits or combines power; the branch plane sets E-plane or H-plane behaviour, and a magic tee combines both with matched arms.
chapters.depth: E-plane tee (series tee) and H-plane tee (shunt tee): branch plane relative to electric field; port numbering; ideal S-matrix properties; lossless 3-port cannot be matched at all ports. Magic tee as E-H tee: H-arm in-phase split, E-arm opposite-phase split, isolation between E and H arms and between collinear arms. Some syllabi group corners, bends and twists with waveguide junctions; give one line each as standard hardware. Derive only the ideal magic-tee S-matrix; keep general tee algebra short.

figure.aria: Magic tee: H-arm feeds collinear ports in phase, E-arm feeds them with opposite signs, and E and H arms are isolated.

chapters.example: An ideal magic tee has 10 mW fed into the H-arm; the E-arm and both collinear arms are matched. Find the power at each collinear port and at the E-arm. Answer: 5 mW at each collinear port, in phase; 0 mW at the E-arm.
chapters.trap: Treating a magic tee as a matched 3-port; swapping E-arm and H-arm phase behaviour; forgetting isolation between E and H arms.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1: rectangular waveguide TE₁₀ mode; 4.1 S-parameters.
chapters.leave: Leave directional couplers to 4.3 and ferrite circulators to 4.5.

chapters.idea: A directional coupler samples power mainly in one direction, and a hybrid ring gives equal split with a fixed phase relation between outputs.
chapters.depth: Directional coupler ports: input, through, coupled, isolated; coupling C = −20 log|S₃₁|, isolation I = −20 log|S₄₁|, directivity D = I − C; two-hole coupler principle (short; some syllabi ask it); hybrid ring (rat-race) 180° hybrid with 3λg/4 spacing; branch-line 90° hybrid only as a comparison. Use S-parameters. Do not derive field theory of coupling holes.

figure.aria: Four-port directional coupler: input at port 1 gives a through wave at port 2, a coupled wave at port 3 and a small isolated wave at port 4.

chapters.example: A directional coupler is fed with 20 dBm at port 1. Its coupling is 10 dB and directivity is 20 dB. Find the coupled-port power and the isolated-port power. Answer: P₃ = 20 − 10 = 10 dBm (10 mW); isolation = C + D = 30 dB; P₄ = 20 − 30 = −10 dBm (0.1 mW).
chapters.trap: Adding directivity and coupling wrong; using voltage ratio for dB power; forgetting coupled-port phase.
chapters.leave: Leave power dividers to 4.4 and circulators to 4.5.

chapters.idea: Power dividers split power by a designed ratio, while attenuators reduce power by a known number of decibels.
chapters.depth: T-junction divider (lossless but not matched at all ports), resistive divider (matched but lossy), Wilkinson divider equal and unequal split with isolation resistor; attenuators: fixed pad, step attenuator, variable attenuator, matching and power rating; dB addition. Some syllabi link this to RF system design filters, couplers and power dividers; keep system level to one line. Do not cover filter design.

figure.aria: Wilkinson divider: input splits through two quarter-wave branches to two outputs, with an isolation resistor between the outputs.

chapters.example: A 20 dBm source passes through a 6 dB attenuator and then an ideal equal Wilkinson divider. Find the power at each output port. Answer: 20 − 6 − 3 = 11 dBm at each output (about 12.6 mW).
chapters.trap: Adding 3 dB split to voltage; thinking a Wilkinson divider is lossless when outputs are mismatched; forgetting attenuator pads match both ports.
chapters.leave: Leave couplers to 4.3, ferrite devices to 4.5 and RF filters to Unit 5.

chapters.idea: Ferrite material under a DC magnetic bias breaks reciprocity, so microwave power can be isolated, circulated or phase-shifted in one chosen direction.
chapters.depth: Ferrite Faraday rotation under DC bias; isolator (forward low loss, reverse high isolation), 3-port Y-junction circulator with S-matrix, 4-port circulator, phase shifter (reciprocal and nonreciprocal); gyrator one line; radar duplexer use. Only a few universities teach detailed ferrite material physics; keep it to rotation and device behaviour. Do not derive tensor permeability.

figure.aria: Three-port circulator: power flows 1→2→3→1 with low loss, while the reverse direction is isolated by the ferrite bias.

chapters.example: A 3-port circulator has insertion loss 0.5 dB and isolation 25 dB. Find the power at ports 2 and 3 when 10 dBm enters port 1. Answer: P₂ = 10 − 0.5 = 9.5 dBm; P₃ = 10 − 25 = −15 dBm.
chapters.trap: Drawing circulation direction wrong; using an isolator as a reciprocal device; forgetting matched loads on unused ports.
chapters.leave: Leave tee and coupler S-matrices to 4.2–4.3; leave radar duplexer system use to Unit 6.

chapters.idea: Microwave tubes use electron beams with cavities or slow-wave structures to generate or amplify high power at high frequency.
chapters.depth: Two-cavity klystron: velocity modulation, drift bunching, output cavity; reflex klystron oscillator: repeller and transit-time mode; magnetron: crossed electric and magnetic fields, π-mode, cavity resonators; TWT: helix slow-wave structure, broadband gain. Compare gain, bandwidth, efficiency and use. Only a few universities teach full reflex-mode theory; keep to mode number and tuning. Do not cover electron optics.

figure.aria: Two-cavity klystron: an electron gun sends a beam through an input cavity, a drifting bunching tube, an output cavity and a collector.

chapters.example: A two-cavity klystron has beam voltage 2 kV, beam current 50 mA and output power 40 W. Find the DC input power and efficiency. Answer: Pdc = 2000 × 0.05 = 100 W; η = 40/100 = 40%.
chapters.trap: Confusing a klystron amplifier with a reflex klystron oscillator; mixing magnetron π-mode with other modes; ignoring TWT broadband trade-off.
chapters.leave: Leave solid-state sources to 4.7 and radar transmitter use to Unit 6.

chapters.idea: Semiconductor negative-resistance and transit-time effects generate microwave power at low voltage without a heated electron beam.
chapters.depth: Gunn diode: transferred-electron effect, negative differential resistance, cavity-controlled oscillation; IMPATT: avalanche multiplication plus transit-time drift, Read diode as its basis; TRAPATT: trapped-plasma mode, high efficiency at lower frequency; tunnel diode: quantum tunnelling, negative resistance, low power. Some syllabi add BARITT and varactor; BARITT as a short comparison, varactor belongs to Unit 5. Only a few universities teach TRAPATT plasma details; keep short.

figure.aria: Four solid-state microwave sources are biased and coupled to a cavity, which sets the output frequency and delivers RF power.

chapters.example: A Gunn diode oscillates at 10 GHz with 8 V supply and 0.5 A current; RF output is 1 W. Find the DC input power and efficiency. Answer: Pdc = 8 × 0.5 = 4 W; η = 1/4 = 25%.
chapters.trap: Calling a Gunn diode a p-n junction; mixing IMPATT avalanche action with Gunn transferred-electron action; expecting a tunnel diode to give high power.
chapters.leave: Leave varactor tuning to Unit 5, RF power amplifiers to Unit 5 and radar use to Unit 6.

chapters.idea: Microwave quantities are measured indirectly with slotted lines, power sensors, wavemeters and calibrated network analysers.
chapters.depth: VSWR by slotted line: Vmax, Vmin, |Γ| = (Vmax − Vmin)/(Vmax + Vmin), VSWR = Vmax/Vmin, λg from twice the distance between minima; power measurement: bolometer, thermistor, thermocouple, directional coupler; frequency: cavity wavemeter, counter; network analyser: S-parameter measurement, SOLT calibration, error correction. Keep detector square-law and calibration as the depth limit. Do not teach antenna measurement.

figure.aria: Slotted-line VSWR measurement: a probe samples the standing wave along a slotted line and a detector drives a meter.

chapters.example: A slotted line gives Vmax = 5 V and Vmin = 1 V at 10 GHz. The distance between successive minima is 15 mm. Find VSWR, reflection coefficient and guide wavelength. Answer: VSWR = 5/1 = 5; |Γ| = (5−1)/(5+1) = 0.667; λg = 2 × 15 mm = 30 mm.
chapters.trap: Using the distance between adjacent minima as λg; forgetting the square-law detector; taking uncalibrated VNA data as final.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1: VSWR and standing waves; 4.1 S-parameters.
chapters.leave: Leave antenna gain and pattern measurements to Unit 3; leave radar range measurements to Unit 6.

chapters.idea: Planar microwave integrated circuits put passive and active components on one substrate, and MMICs make the whole circuit monolithic.
chapters.depth: Hybrid MIC and monolithic MIC (MMIC); substrates alumina, GaAs, InP, Si; microstrip and CPW; resistors, capacitors, inductors, airbridges; MMIC advantages (small, repeatable, broadband) and disadvantages (low power, expensive setup); packaging; RF system design links to filters, couplers, dividers, LNAs and PAs in Unit 5. Only a few universities teach detailed fabrication; keep process to a short sequence. Do not design RFIC layouts.
chapters.example: A MMIC power amplifier has gain 10 dB and output 1 dB compression at 18 dBm. Input is 10 dBm. Find the linear output and the actual output. Answer: linear output = 10 + 10 = 20 dBm; saturation at 18 dBm limits the actual output to 18 dBm, so it is compressed by 2 dB.
chapters.trap: Confusing hybrid MIC with MMIC; ignoring substrate loss and parasitics; thinking on-chip inductors are ideal.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1: microstrip and stripline; 4.1 S-parameters; Unit 5: RF passive components and amplifiers.
chapters.leave: Leave RFIC layout and detailed fabrication to advanced study; leave LNA and PA design to Unit 5.
